query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating machine‐learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) with thermodynamic integration (akin to TOR-TILD) will retain key entropy and anharmonicity features in free energy evaluations while dramatically reducing computational cost compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary systems (and, with cautious extension, select high-entropy alloys) at high temperatures near the fusion point.
generation.intervention: Develop and employ an MLIP trained on selectively sampled ab initio data that targets crucial atomic configurations from both solid and liquid states. Use this MLIP within a thermodynamic integration framework to compute phase free energies and entropy contributions instead of full AIMD trajectories.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions spanning the melting point of the material in question. For initial tests, systems where previous TOR-TILD and AIMD data exist (e.g. elemental or binary systems) will be used to benchmark performance and fidelity.
generation.structural_mediator: The local atomic environment descriptors captured by the MLIP, which encode anharmonic vibrations, electron–vibration coupling, and configurational entropy effects critical to the free energy landscape around melting.
generation.mechanism: By training the MLIP on a carefully chosen subset of ab initio data that encompasses the relevant fluctuations and anharmonic effects, the potential can predict forces and energies with high fidelity. When integrated via thermodynamic integration, this approach should reproduce the free energy and associated entropy terms of both phases efficiently, while avoiding the computational overhead of full AIMD.
generation.predicted_outcome: The MLIP-based workflow is predicted to yield free energy evaluations (and subsequently fusion properties) with accuracy comparable to AIMD/TOR-TILD (e.g., within roughly 10% of melting temperatures and free energy values) but with computational costs reduced by an order of magnitude or more, particularly making multicomponent systems more tractable.
generation.baseline: Current explicit AIMD workflows and TOR-TILD methods which are accurate but computationally expensive for multicomponent high-entropy systems, and where obtaining complete free energy landscapes (including vibrational entropy and anharmonicity) demands extensive MD sampling.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be most effective for elemental and binary systems near their melting points. Its extension to multicomponent or extremely anharmonic systems might require more rigorous active learning schemes and additional validation. Systems with very strong electron–vibration coupling where MLIP training data may be sparse might also present challenges.
generation.uncertainty: While promising, it remains uncertain whether MLIPs can capture all subtleties of electron–vibration coupling and extreme anharmonic behavior across all material systems. The performance gain in very complex, multicomponent high-entropy systems has yet to be demonstrated.

falsification_experiment.design: Train an MLIP on a representative dataset obtained from ab initio calculations for a well-characterized elemental or binary system near its melting point. Use the MLIP in a thermodynamic integration framework to compute the free energies of both the solid and liquid phases, and derive melting properties. Benchmark these predictions against full AIMD and TOR-TILD evaluations.
measurements: Quantitative free energy differences for both phases across a range of temperatures
Predicted melting (fusion) temperature and associated entropy contributions
Computational time and resources required by the MLIP-based workflow versus AIMD/TOR-TILD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP-based approach yields free energy values or melting temperatures that deviate by more than approximately 10% from those obtained via explicit AIMD/TOR-TILD, or if the computational speed-up is less than a factor of 2 relative to AIMD, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
